inventory what all superfunctions needs an admin UI (compare with equivalent commercial Platform as a service...) like better-auth, clerk, descope, auth0 for authfn, resend for sendfn etc...

do it as fast as possible

I’ll do this as a read-only inventory, in parallel: one pass over every function in the repo, one mapping to current commercial equivalents, and one pass focused on the minimum admin capabilities each product category actually exposes. I’ll return a prioritized matrix, not a generic “everything needs a dashboard” answer.

The repo contains 35 tracked `*fn` products—substantially more than the small root README table—so I’m treating the directory inventory as authoritative and separating “must-have operator console” from “nice visual inspector” and “library/workbench only.” Early signal: the stateful control planes (identity, billing, data/files, integrations, delivery, workflows, observability, hosting) are the clear first wave.

Inventory is complete. The key correction to the obvious first answer is architectural: there are 36 product directories, but you should not create 20+ separate admin applications. The right shape is one authenticated Superfunctions Console with product modules; several functions explicitly belong inside another module (for example, LogFn and CatchFn under WatchFn, ContentFn under CmsFn).

The PaaS answer: **21 of 36 Superfunctions need an admin surface, 6 would benefit from an inspector/workbench, and 9 should not have a standalone admin UI.**

Build **one modular Superfunctions Console**, not 21 separate dashboards. This is a read-only source inventory of `next` at `8dddd865`; I did not run the existing UIs.

Commercial platforms consistently expose projects/environments, credentials, operational resources, runs/events, logs, analytics and recovery actions—see [Auth0](https://auth0.com/docs/get-started/auth0-overview/dashboard), [Stripe](https://docs.stripe.com/dashboard/basics), [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/projects), [Resend](https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/emails/introduction), [Inngest](https://www.inngest.com/docs/platform/monitor/inspecting-function-runs) and [Algolia](https://www.algolia.com/doc/guides/search-analytics/overview).

## Core admin modules — 21

These need an admin UI to compete as self-hosted PaaS products.

| Function | Commercial product shape | Minimum admin surface |
|---|---|---|
| `authfn` | Clerk, Better Auth, Descope, Auth0 | Users, identities, organizations, roles, sessions, MFA, API keys, providers, impersonation, blocking/deletion, audit |
| `billfn` | Stripe Billing, Paddle, RevenueCat | Customers, catalog/prices, subscriptions, entitlements, meters, invoices, credits, coupons, dunning, revenue |
| `browsefn` | Browserbase, Browserless, Apify | Browser/crawl jobs, live sessions, recordings, artifacts, provider keys, concurrency, rate limits, usage |
| `catchfn` | Sentry Feedback, Jam, Marker.io | Bug inbox, screenshots, breadcrumbs, repro evidence, severity, assignment, issue sync—inside WatchFn |
| `cifn` | GitHub Actions, CircleCI, Buildkite | Pipelines, runs/jobs, runners, logs, artifacts, secrets, schedules, retry/cancel |
| `cmsfn` | [Contentful](https://www.contentful.com/help/getting-started/contentful-web-app-overview/), [Sanity Studio](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio) | Content types, documents, drafts, assets, previews, publishing, releases, collaboration and roles |
| `compfn` | [Vanta](https://help.vanta.com/en/articles/11690312-audit-101-how-audits-work), Drata | Frameworks, controls, evidence, checks, risks, exceptions, owners, auditors and exports |
| `datafn` | [Supabase](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/overview), Firebase, Hasura | Schema/table browser, records, query console, sync clients/conflicts, RBAC, keys, migrations, backups, performance |
| `filefn` | [Cloudinary](https://cloudinary.com/documentation/media_library_for_developers), UploadThing | Files, folders, versions, upload sessions, transformations, access grants, quotas, retention and recovery |
| `flowfn` | [Inngest](https://www.inngest.com/docs/platform/replay), Temporal, Trigger.dev | Queues, streams, workflows, workers, schedules, execution graph, retries, replay/cancel and DLQ |
| `hostfn` | [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/deployments/managing-deployments), Render, Railway | Projects, environments, deployments, logs, domains, certificates, variables/secrets, health, traffic and rollback |
| `mailfn` | MailSlurp, Mailtrap, AgentMail, [Resend Receiving](https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/receiving/introduction) | Inboxes, messages, threads, raw MIME, attachments, domains/routes, credentials, webhooks, retention and abuse controls |
| `memoryfn` | Mem0, Zep | Tenants/agents, memories, sources, search, graph/conflicts, retention, consent, deletion, usage and cost |
| `plugfn` | Nango, Paragon, [Pipedream Connect](https://pipedream.com/docs/connect/managed-auth/users) | Provider catalog, OAuth apps, end-user connections, credentials, scopes, webhooks, sync/workflow runs and retries |
| `recfn` | Recall.ai, Fireflies | Bots, meetings, participants, recordings, transcripts, consent, platform/ASR config, webhooks, failures and retention |
| `searchfn` | [Algolia](https://www.algolia.com/doc/guides/search-analytics/overview), Elastic Cloud, Typesense | Collections, schema, documents, ingestion, relevance rules, synonyms, analytics, keys, snapshots and usage |
| `secfn` | Doppler, Infisical, Snyk | Secrets and versions, environments, RBAC, policies, rotation, scanners/findings, approvals, incidents and audit |
| `sendfn` | [Resend](https://resend.com/docs/cli), Postmark, Twilio, Novu | Providers, domains/senders, templates, messages, delivery events, suppressions, webhooks, API keys and usage |
| `testfn` | BrowserStack, Sauce Labs | Projects, suites/cases, runs, failures, flaky trends, agents/environments, artifacts and visual baselines |
| `userfn` | [LaunchDarkly](https://launchdarkly.com/docs/home/flags/manage), Intercom, Canny | Users/segments, flags and targeting, campaigns, surveys, feedback, roadmap, changelog and analytics |
| `watchfn` | [Datadog](https://docs.datadoghq.com/logs/explorer/), Sentry, New Relic | Services, metrics, traces, logs, errors, RUM, dashboards, monitors, incidents, alerts, retention and keys |

## Useful or conditional — 6

| Function | Comparable to | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| `apifn` | Postman, Stoplight, SwaggerHub | API catalog, spec diff, collections, environments, mocks and test history; useful, but CLI/components can launch first |
| `botfn` | Botpress | Bot/channel configuration, credentials, conversations and failures; required only as a hosted multi-bot platform |
| `cachefn` | [Upstash](https://upstash.com/docs/redis/howto/metrics-and-charts), RedisInsight | Key/TTL inspector, hit ratio, hot keys, eviction, purge/warm and capacity; becomes core when distributed |
| `docsfn` | Mintlify, ReadMe, GitBook | Build/preview/deploy, domains, search analytics and feedback; can remain code-first |
| `langfn` | [LangSmith](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/dashboards), Braintrust | Traces, prompts, datasets, evaluations, token costs and feedback; core only if positioned as an LLM operations platform |
| `probefn` | Playwright Trace Viewer, Percy, Checkly | Local session/artifact/baseline/diff viewer; does not initially require a hosted control plane |

## No standalone admin UI — 9

| Function | Why |
|---|---|
| `chartfn` | Rendering library like ECharts/Highcharts; gallery/playground belongs in docs |
| `clifn` | CLI primitives like oclif/Commander |
| `contentfn` | Headless content engine; **CmsFn Studio should administer it** |
| `drawfn` | The canvas is its end-user product UI |
| `extfn` | Framework like Plasmo/WXT; each generated extension owns its UI |
| `iconfn` | Icon asset library; needs a browser/catalog, not administration |
| `logfn` | Structured emitter/transport; **WatchFn should own log exploration** |
| `mcpfn` | Protocol/conformance SDK; MCP hosts or inspectors should own interactive UI |
| `uifn` | Component system; Storybook/catalog/workbench is the correct interface |

## Current implementation reality

- **CiFn** already has a genuine dashboard with runs, details, logs, artifacts and login routes: [App.tsx](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/cifn/typescript/dashboard/src/App.tsx:11).
- **CmsFn** has Studio source, but its package still describes it as a boot skeleton: [package.json](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/cmsfn/studio/package.json:2).
- **WatchFn** is currently hard-coded prototype data with a literal chart placeholder: [page.tsx](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/watchfn/dashboard/src/app/page.tsx:11).
- **AuthFn** has admin HTTP operations, currently only `users.list` and `users.delete`, not a visual console: [index.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/authfn/admin/src/index.ts:21).
- **UIFn’s** AuthFn/PlugFn/FileFn/BillFn panels are customer-facing settings patterns, not cross-tenant administration: [shared.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions/uifn/sf/src/shared.ts:3).
- CatchFn and LogFn already point operational UI responsibility toward WatchFn; ContentFn delegates Studio responsibility to CmsFn; McpFn deliberately stays below product-level inspectors.

## Recommended console architecture

Create one shell providing:

- Tenant → project → environment switching
- AuthFn-backed RBAC, MFA and support impersonation
- Global audit history and approval workflows
- API keys, secrets, redaction and rotation
- Shared run/event/log timeline with retry, replay and cancellation
- Global search, saved filters, bulk actions and exports
- Usage, quota, cost, retention and backup controls
- Strong confirmations and recovery for destructive operations

Then mount product modules. Fold `catchfn` and `logfn` into WatchFn, `contentfn` into CmsFn, and port the existing CiFn dashboard into the shell. Use UIFn for the shared visual system, but keep customer portals distinct from operator administration.

Suggested order: **Console shell + AuthFn/audit → WatchFn backbone → PlugFn/SendFn/MailFn/BillFn/FileFn → DataFn/FlowFn/HostFn/SecFn/SearchFn → remaining vertical modules.**

```mermaid
flowchart LR

```

All four surfaces should reuse the same authorization, validation, redaction, idempotency and audit logic. I recommend one aggregate Super Console MCP server that mounts tools only for enabled modules, while still allowing a function’s tool pack to be mounted independently.

Before I create anything, I need these decisions:

1. **Execution scope:** When you say “work the entire thing out at once,” do you mean full production implementation for all 21 core admin modules in this worktree—not merely the architecture, contracts and first vertical slice?

2. **Product layout:** I recommend a top-level `superconsole/` composition product, not `consolefn`, containing packages such as `@superconsole/core`, `web`, `server`, `sdk`, `mcp` and `cli`. Confirm?

3. **Web stack:** I recommend React powered entirely by UIFn, with a framework-neutral server using `@superfunctions/http`. This also makes the existing React CiFn dashboard easiest to absorb. Use React/Vite, React/Next.js, or another stack?

4. **Module selection:** I recommend explicit deploy-time registration through `superconsole.config.ts` and CLI commands such as `superconsole add authfn`. 5. **Coverage:** Should v1 implement:

   - Only the 21 required modules, leaving extension points for the optional six?

6. **Admin packages:** I recommend each function owns an admin package—following the existing `@authfn/admin` precedent—with:

   - Admin domain service and capability manifest

   - Typed TypeScript client
   - MCP tool descriptors/handlers

7. **MCP permissions:** I recommend read operations enabled according to AuthFn scopes, while mutations and destructive tools require explicit deployment enablement, stronger scopes, idempotency keys, confirmation metadata and immutable audit entries. Confirm?

8. **Tenancy:** Should the universal hierarchy be `organization/workspace → project → environment`, multi-tenant from day one, even for self-hosted installations? Recommended: yes, with AuthFn identity/RBAC and SecFn secrets.

11. **Compatibility:** May the new admin contracts make clean breaking changes where useful, while leaving existing non-admin public SDKs intact?

12. **Deployment posture:** Self-hosted-first but architected for a future hosted 21n Super Console, or strictly self-hosted?

const description = `## Executive summary

Build **Super Console**, the modular self-hosted administration control plane for the Superfunctions ecosystem. A deployment explicitly registers the Superfunctions it uses, and the console exposes only those enabled product modules across navigation, UI routes, REST/OpenAPI, TypeScript admin clients, and MCP.

## Problem

Superfunctions currently expose uneven operator surfaces: CiFn has a standalone React dashboard, CmsFn has an early Studio shell, WatchFn has a placeholder dashboard, AuthFn has limited admin routes, and most functions have no coherent administration UI or stable admin API. Consumers need one composable operator experience without conflating operator administration with customer-facing portals.

## Desired outcome

A production-quality, self-hosted Super Console built at \`superconsole/\` with SvelteKit, Tailwind, and UIFn. Each function owns an admin capability manifest and service contract; the console mounts selected modules, shared administration APIs, TypeScript clients, OpenAPI descriptions, and McpFn-backed tools. The universal tenancy model is organization/workspace → project → environment.

## Scope

### Shared platform

- SvelteKit console shell powered by UIFn; repair UIFn at source when gaps or defects are found. Workarounds and parallel visual systems are prohibited.
- Explicit deploy-time module registration and capability discovery. Disabled modules must not appear or remain addressable through UI, REST, OpenAPI, or MCP.
- AuthFn-powered operator identity, sessions, tenancy, RBAC, and service authentication.
- Audited mutations and shared audit-event contracts; use the relevant Superfunction for each platform concern rather than duplicating substitute implementations.
- Versioned language-neutral REST API and generated OpenAPI.
- TypeScript admin SDK generated or composed from stable contracts.
- McpFn-backed discoverable admin tools, including scoped and audited mutations.
- Shared organization/workspace, project, environment, module, navigation, search, notification, usage, and error primitives.
- Port the existing CiFn dashboard behavior into the shell.

### Required product modules

AuthFn, BillFn, BrowseFn, CiFn, CmsFn, CompFn, DataFn, FileFn, FlowFn, HostFn, MailFn, MemoryFn, PlugFn, RecFn, SearchFn, SecFn, SendFn, TestFn, UserFn, and WatchFn.

CatchFn and LogFn are owned by WatchFn modules. ContentFn is owned by CmsFn.

### Optional product modules

ApiFn, BotFn, CacheFn, DocsFn, LangFn, and ProbeFn. They use the same capability contract and are enabled only when configured.

## Hard architecture rules

1. UIFn is the sole shared visual system for the operator console.
2. Customer-facing portals remain distinct from operator administration.
3. Every product module consumes its function-owned admin service/capability contract; the console may compose but must not redefine domain logic.
4. Relevant Superfunctions power console concerns—for example AuthFn for identity/RBAC, McpFn for MCP exposure, WatchFn/LogFn/CatchFn for observability, SecFn for security controls, and FileFn for managed artifacts.
5. Admin REST paths are versioned, described by OpenAPI, and consumable independently of the console.
6. The TypeScript admin SDK and MCP tools preserve the same authorization, scope, validation, error, pagination, idempotency, and audit semantics as REST.
7. Disabled modules are absent from every exposure surface.
8. Existing non-admin SDK compatibility is preserved; breaking changes are allowed only in unfinished admin APIs where necessary.

## Non-goals

- A hosted Superfunctions cloud control plane.
- Python admin SDKs in this delivery.
- Standalone admin applications for ChartFn, CliFn, DrawFn, ExtFn, IconFn, LogFn, McpFn, or UIFn.
- A separate ContentFn console.
- Merging end-customer portals into operator administration.
- Pushing a branch or opening a pull request as part of this local implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- \`superconsole/\` provides a working self-hosted SvelteKit console shell, configuration model, tenancy selector, module registry, RBAC guards, navigation, routing, error states, and audit visibility.
- All 21 required and 6 optional modules are implemented through real capability manifests and usable operator views; CatchFn/LogFn are nested in WatchFn and ContentFn is nested in CmsFn.
- CiFn dashboard capabilities are ported to the shell rather than embedded as a second application.
- Only explicitly enabled modules appear or respond through UI, REST/OpenAPI, TypeScript SDK, and MCP.
- Function-owned administration contracts cover their operator objects and mutations, with consistent validation, pagination, errors, idempotency, authorization, and audit metadata.
- OpenAPI and TypeScript admin SDK surfaces are generated/verified and usable without the console.
- McpFn exposes equivalent scoped tools; mutations are authorization-checked and audited.
- UIFn source changes cover every shared UI need discovered during implementation, with no one-off visual-system bypasses.
- Local architecture, capability inventory, rules, API/MCP model, security/tenancy model, module rollout, testing, operations, and decision records live under \`superconsole/.conduct/SFN-<id>/\` after issue creation.
- Automated tests cover registry filtering, authorization, tenancy isolation, route/API/MCP exposure, audit emission, representative module behavior, and the migrated CiFn workflows.
- Build, typecheck, lint, unit, integration, and relevant UI checks pass.
- Work is kept local in an isolated exact-head worktree with coherent separate commits and no push/PR.

## Dependencies

UIFn, AuthFn, McpFn, WatchFn, LogFn, CatchFn, SecFn, DataFn, FileFn, the shared HTTP/database packages, and function-specific domain services. Existing CiFn dashboard behavior is the migration source.

## Risks and mitigations

- **Uneven function maturity:** define a strict common capability contract and implement real domain-adapter boundaries rather than placeholder pages.
- **Authorization drift across surfaces:** one policy decision and request context must govern UI, REST, SDK, and MCP.
- **Accidental module exposure:** derive all routes, schemas, tools, and navigation from the validated deployment registry.
- **UI inconsistency:** enforce UIFn imports and fix missing primitives in UIFn itself.
- **Cross-tenant leakage:** require explicit tenant/project/environment scope and isolation tests for every request.
- **Large delivery surface:** use parallel non-overlapping implementation tracks, contract tests, and coherent local commits.

## Open questions

No product decisions are blocking implementation. Low-level implementation details will be recorded as architecture decisions and validated against the current repository during delivery.`;

+# SFN-21 — Super Console
+
+This bundle is the source-controlled architecture and delivery record for [SFN-21](https://linear.app/21n/issue/SFN-21/build-super-console-as-the-modular-self-hosted-administration-control).
+
+Super Console is the self-hosted operator control plane for a consumer-selected set of Superfunctions. A deployment registers modules explicitly. That registry is the only source for console navigation, server dispatch, REST/OpenAPI, the TypeScript admin client, and McpFn tool discovery. A function that is not registered is absent from every surface.
+
+## Binding decisions
+
+- Product and directory: **Super Console**, `superconsole/`.
+- Runtime: self-hosted SvelteKit.
+- Visual system: Tailwind configured through UIFn, with `@uifn/components-svelte` as the component boundary.
+- UIFn defects or missing primitives are fixed in UIFn; local substitutes and secondary component libraries are prohibited.
+- Relevant Superfunctions must power their corresponding console concern instead of local reimplementations.
+- Operator administration stays separate from customer portals and embedded product UI.
+- Each function owns its administration service interface and capability manifest.
+- REST is versioned and language-neutral; OpenAPI is generated from enabled capabilities.
+- The initial admin SDK is TypeScript.
+- McpFn projects enabled capabilities to MCP; mutations use the same scope, policy, validation, idempotency, and audit path as REST.
+- Tenancy is organization/workspace → project → environment.
+- CatchFn and LogFn are nested under WatchFn. ContentFn is nested under CmsFn.
+- CiFn's existing React dashboard behavior is migrated into the SvelteKit shell.
+- Delivery remains local in coherent commits; no push or pull request is part of SFN-21.
+

+# Product rationale
+
+## Thesis
+
+Superfunctions should compose as one platform without collapsing into one runtime. Super Console supplies a consistent operator surface while functions retain domain ownership. It serves human operators through SvelteKit, application developers through REST/OpenAPI and a TypeScript client, and agents through McpFn.
+
+## Problem
+
+Before SFN-21, operator support was uneven:
+
+- CiFn had an isolated React dashboard for runs, job logs, and artifacts.
+- CmsFn had a Studio package centered on content authoring.
+- WatchFn had a dashboard package with hard-coded prototype data.
+- AuthFn exposed only a small set of framework-neutral admin routes.
+- most functions had SDKs, CLIs, specifications, or planned dashboards but no coherent administration plane.
+
+Building a separate dashboard for every function would duplicate authentication, tenant selection, authorization, audit, layout, accessibility, API semantics, deployment, and maintenance. It would also make cross-function investigation unnecessarily fragmented.
+
+## Users and jobs
+
+### Installation owner
+
+- register exactly the functions deployed in the installation;
+- configure workspaces, projects, environments, identity, access, providers, secrets, domains, quotas, retention, and integrations;
+- inspect health, usage, cost, incidents, and audit history;
+- upgrade or disable a function without leaving a stale UI, API path, schema, or MCP tool.
+
+### Operator and support engineer
+
+- find permitted resources across enabled modules;
+- correlate runs, workflows, messages, deliveries, logs, traces, recordings, files, deployments, and incidents;
+- execute safe retries, cancellations, rotations, purges, replays, rollbacks, and repairs;
+- receive a stable audit receipt for every mutation.
+
+### Developer and automation author
+
+- consume stable administration operations without scraping a console;
+- use identical pagination, validation, errors, authorization, and idempotency through REST, TypeScript, and MCP;
+- discover installation capabilities at runtime.
+
+### Auditor
+
+- inspect grants, policy decisions, mutations, evidence, findings, exceptions, configuration history, retention, and security events in a stable tenant scope.
+
+## Product principles
+
+1. **Selected means exposed.** Only registered modules exist on any surface.
+2. **The function owns the domain.** The shell composes; it does not redefine business logic.
+3. **One dispatch path.** UI, REST, SDK, and MCP share policy, validation, execution, and audit.
+4. **Self-hosted first.** No Superfunctions-hosted control plane is required.
+5. **Human and agent parity.** Safe console operations have API and MCP equivalents.
+6. **UIFn or improve UIFn.** Visual-system gaps are fixed at their source.
+7. **Use Superfunctions to operate Superfunctions.** Identity, MCP, observability, security, data, files, and other concerns use their owning packages.
+8. **Operator UI is not customer UI.** Customer portals and widgets remain separate products.
+9. **Safe mutations are a contract.** Scope, permission, confirmation, validation, idempotency, and audit are declared rather than page-specific behavior.
+10. **Complexity follows deployment.** A small installation sees a small console.
+
+## Success conditions
+
+- adding a function does not require new shell routing logic;
+- disabling a function removes all five projections: UI, dispatch, REST/OpenAPI, SDK discovery, and MCP;
+- representative operator work is possible for every required and optional module;
+- console, REST, SDK, and MCP return the same result and audit identity;
+- tenancy isolation and permission tests cover every dispatcher entry;
+- CiFn workflows remain usable after migration;
+- UIFn is the only operator visual system;
+- installation, backup, upgrade, and troubleshooting are documented for self-hosters.
+
+## Boundaries
+
+SFN-21 does not build a hosted SaaS, a Python admin SDK, or standalone admin products for component/rendering libraries. It does not merge customer billing portals, auth widgets, feedback widgets, or file pickers into operator administration. Stable non-admin SDKs remain compatible.

+# Architecture
+
+## Core invariant
+
+One validated deployment registry projects the enabled system into five synchronized surfaces:
+
+```text
+function-owned admin services and manifests
+                    │
+                    ▼
+        @superfunctions/admin registry
+       ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
+       ▼            ▼             ▼
+ SvelteKit UI   REST/OpenAPI   McpFn tools
+                    │
+                    ▼
+           TypeScript admin SDK
+```
+
+The registry must make the following true by construction:
+
+1. disabled modules are neither discoverable nor addressable;
+2. every surface uses identical authentication, scope, policy, schema validation, domain execution, normalized error, idempotency, and audit behavior;
+3. Super Console depends on transport-neutral function contracts, while functions do not depend on SvelteKit.
+
+## Layers
+
+### Function-owned domain administration
+
+Every function's `admin` package declares:
+
+- operator resources and identifiers;
+- list, get, mutation, and domain-action service methods;
+- JSON schemas for input and output;
+- tenant scope and permissions;
+- safety, confirmation, and idempotency metadata;
+- audit action and target metadata;
+- health and related-resource signals;
+- an adapter factory that delegates to an injected domain service.
+
+The package does not create fake product data or embed framework-specific handlers.
+
+### Shared administration kernel
+
+`@superfunctions/admin` supplies:
+
+- manifest types and validation;
+- dependency and nested-ownership resolution;
+- the enabled-module registry;
+- request and tenant context;
+- authentication and authorization interfaces compatible with AuthFn;
+- policy enforcement;
+- schema validation;
+- cursor pagination and normalized errors;
+- idempotency coordination;
+- domain dispatch;
+- sanitized audit emission;
+- OpenAPI 3.1 generation;
+- McpFn-compatible tool projection and invocation;
+- a fetch-based TypeScript administration client.
+
+It is transport-neutral and has no Svelte dependency.
+
+### Super Console composition server
+
+The SvelteKit server:
+
+- loads explicit server-only installation configuration;
+- binds real function service adapters to manifests;
+- creates the registry and shared dispatcher;
+- resolves AuthFn actors and canonical tenant context;
+- exposes versioned REST, OpenAPI, MCP, registry, audit, search, and settings endpoints;
+- supplies view models to Svelte routes;
+- fails startup on invalid dependencies, collisions, or unsafe capability declarations.
+
+### UIFn presentation
+
+Svelte routes consume view models and operation links from the registry. They do not import domain storage. Shared interaction patterns come from UIFn. Module presentation code may compose UIFn primitives but may not fork them.
+
+## Registry validation
+
+Startup validation rejects:
+
+- duplicate module, resource, operation, route, OpenAPI operation, or MCP tool identifiers;
+- dependency cycles or missing required modules;
+- a nested module whose declared parent is absent;
+- conflicting route patterns;
+- mutations without permission and audit metadata;
+- destructive operations without explicit safety metadata;
+- idempotent operations without a defined key strategy;
+- invalid scope declarations;
+- navigation entries for nested-only modules;
+- capability schema versions unsupported by the kernel.
+
+Validation fails closed before the server accepts requests.
+
+## Deployment registration
+
+Modules are enabled by a typed server-only manifest. Environment variables may select a configuration file or supply secrets, but the presence of a credential never silently enables a module.
+
+Conceptually:
+
+```ts
+createSuperConsole({
+  modules: [
+    authAdmin({ service: authService }),
+    watchAdmin({
+      service: watchService,
+      catchService,
+      logService
+    }),
+    ciAdmin({ service: ciService })
+  ]
+});
+```
+
+A disabled-module request returns canonical not-found behavior so installation composition is not disclosed.
+
+## Request lifecycle
+
+1. authenticate the actor using AuthFn-backed session or service credentials;
+2. resolve organization/workspace, project, and environment context;
+3. locate an enabled operation in the registry;
+4. evaluate declared permission and contextual policy;
+5. validate request input;
+6. enforce confirmation and idempotency when applicable;
+7. invoke the function-owned adapter;
+8. sanitize and append the audit event;
+9. emit structured WatchFn/LogFn telemetry;
+10. return the normalized result and audit identity.
+
+UI server actions, REST handlers, SDK requests, and McpFn calls enter at step one and converge before step three.
+
+## Failure behavior
+
+- Unknown or disabled module/operation: not found.
+- Missing identity: unauthenticated.
+- Invalid tenant selection: not found when disclosure would leak membership, otherwise forbidden.
+- Policy denial: forbidden with a stable reason code.
+- Schema failure: validation error with field issues.
+- Idempotency collision: conflict.
+- Domain conflict: normalized conflict preserving safe domain metadata.
+- Dependency unavailable: service unavailable with retry guidance.
+- Unexpected failure: opaque internal error with request ID; detailed data stays in server telemetry.
+
+Secrets, tokens, raw credentials, private message bodies, and configured redaction fields never enter generic error or audit envelopes.
+
+## Persistence
+
+The kernel defines interfaces rather than a mandatory database. Self-hosters bind supported DataFn or `@superfunctions/db` adapters. A function that accepts a shared database adapter wraps it with its own schema and namespace before use, consistent with repository rules.
+
+Audit and idempotency stores must be durable in multi-process deployments. In-memory implementations are permitted only in tests or explicitly single-process development mode.

+# Function administration module contract
+
+## Ownership
+
+A function's `admin` package is the source of truth for operator capability. It exports a manifest and a factory that binds an injected domain administration service. Super Console does not discover methods by reflection and does not directly access a function's database.
+
+## Manifest identity
+
+Every manifest has:
+
+- stable lowercase module ID;
+- human title and description;
+- semantic capability version;
+- required or optional classification;
+- standalone or nested presentation mode;
+- dependency module IDs;
+- owning parent for nested modules;
+- supported scope levels;
+- health metadata;
+- resource and operation declarations.
+
+Module IDs are stable API identities, not npm package names. Operation IDs are globally unique after namespacing as `<module>.<resource>.<action>`.
+
+## Resource declaration
+
+A resource declares:
+
+- ID, singular/plural labels, description, icon key, and risk classification;
+- canonical ID field and safe display fields;
+- list/get operation IDs;
+- searchable/filterable/sortable fields;
+- related-resource references;
+- default scope and required permission;
+- whether sensitive fields may be exposed and their redaction policy;
+- navigation or nested placement.
+
+Resources describe administration state, not generic screen layout.
+
+## Operation declaration
+
+An operation declares:
+
+- stable operation ID and summary;
+- read, create, update, delete, or domain-action kind;
+- HTTP method and registry-relative path;
+- input, output, and error JSON schemas;
+- required scope and permission set;
+- safety level: read, safe mutation, sensitive mutation, destructive mutation;
+- confirmation requirements;
+- idempotency mode and key strategy;
+- audit action and target resolver;
+- pagination/filter/sort support;
+- MCP exposure eligibility;
+- deprecation metadata;
+- the injected service handler.
+
+No mutation may omit permission and audit declarations. Destructive actions must be explicit and cannot be inferred from the HTTP method alone.
+
+## Invocation context
+
+The kernel supplies a frozen context containing:
+
+- authenticated actor ID, actor type, and authentication method;
+- workspace, project, environment, and active scope level;
+- effective function namespace and optional region;
+- role grants and policy attributes;
+- request and correlation IDs;
+- source surface: console, REST, SDK, or MCP;
+- locale and time zone;
+- idempotency key where applicable;
+- abort signal.
+
+Handlers may narrow scope but may not expand it. They forward context to the domain service, which remains responsible for object-level authorization and namespace isolation.
+
+## Handler result
+
+Successful handlers return typed data plus optional resource references, warnings, pagination, and safe metadata. They do not construct HTTP responses. The dispatcher attaches request and audit identities.
+
+Domain errors are mapped to canonical admin codes while preserving safe details:
+
+- `invalid_argument`;
+- `unauthenticated`;
+- `forbidden`;
+- `not_found`;
+- `conflict`;
+- `rate_limited`;
+- `precondition_failed`;
+- `dependency_unavailable`;
+- `internal`.
+
+## Audit
+
+Every mutation produces an event with:
+
+- unique audit ID and timestamp;
+- actor and canonical tenant scope;
+- module, operation, action, and target references;
+- source surface;
+- request, correlation, and idempotency IDs;
+- policy decision;
+- sanitized input summary;
+- outcome, normalized error code, and duration;
+- function observation references when supplied.
+
+The manifest provides redaction hints; the kernel applies global secret-key detection as defense in depth.
+
+## Nested ownership
+
+Nested modules register full resources and operations but contribute navigation below their parent. They cannot appear as top-level modules.
+
+- `catchfn` → `watchfn`;
+- `logfn` → `watchfn`;
+- `contentfn` → `cmsfn`.
+
+Disabling a nested module removes its resources, routes, OpenAPI operations, and MCP tools while leaving the parent active.
+
+## Compatibility
+
+Capability versions follow semantic versioning independently of UI releases. Additive resource fields and operations are minor changes. Removed/renamed operations, scope changes, tightened schemas, or different mutation safety are major changes. Deprecation metadata must reach registry discovery, OpenAPI, the TypeScript client, MCP descriptions, and the UI.

+# REST and OpenAPI
+
+## Base paths
+
+- Administration API: `/api/admin/v1`
+- Capability discovery: `/api/admin/v1/registry`
+- Installation overview: `/api/admin/v1/overview`
+- Enabled module operations: `/api/admin/v1/modules/{moduleId}/...`
+- Global search: `/api/admin/v1/search`
+- Audit stream/query: `/api/admin/v1/audit`
+- Installation and module settings: `/api/admin/v1/settings`
+- MCP discovery/configuration: `/api/admin/v1/mcp`
+- OpenAPI 3.1 document: `/api/admin/v1/openapi.json`
+
+Only enabled operations appear in routing and OpenAPI.
+
+## Scope
+
+Canonical scope is carried in route or validated headers according to the deployment adapter. The normalized context contains workspace, project, environment, optional function namespace, and optional region. An installation may bind workspace to organization terminology without changing API field identity.
+
+Scope values are never trusted merely because they were sent by a client. AuthFn membership and the function's object-level authorization are evaluated for each request.
+
+## Envelopes
+
+Success:
+
+```json
+{
+  "ok": true,
+  "data": {},
+  "page": { "nextCursor": null, "hasMore": false },
+  "requestId": "req_...",
+  "auditId": "audit_..."
+}
+```
+
+Failure:
+
+```json
+{
+  "ok": false,
+  "error": {
+    "code": "forbidden",
+    "message": "The active actor cannot perform this operation.",
+    "issues": [],
+    "retryable": false
+  },
+  "requestId": "req_..."
+}
+```
+
+`auditId` is returned for mutations whose execution reached audit recording, including audited failures. Secret or private domain payloads never appear in generic errors.
+
+## Pagination, filtering, and sorting
+
+- Cursor pagination is stable under the resource's declared ordering.
+- Default and maximum page sizes are operation metadata.
+- Filters and sort keys are enumerated by the manifest and reflected in OpenAPI.
+- Unknown filters and sorts are validation errors rather than silently ignored.
+- Cursors are opaque and scope-bound.
+
+## Idempotency and concurrency
+
+- Operations marked idempotent accept `Idempotency-Key`.
+- Keys are scoped to actor, tenant, module, operation, and normalized request identity.
+- Repeated matching requests return the stored outcome and original audit reference.
+- Reusing a key for different input returns conflict.
+- Operations that expose optimistic concurrency use an ETag or declared version token and `If-Match`.
+
+## Authentication
+
+Interactive requests use AuthFn sessions. Automation uses scoped service credentials or API keys. The OpenAPI document declares configured security schemes but never embeds credentials. CSRF rules remain active for cookie-authenticated mutations.
+
+## OpenAPI projection
+
+The generator emits OpenAPI 3.1 with:
+
+- one tag per enabled module and nested grouping metadata;
+- deterministic operation IDs;
+- request, response, page, error, and audit schemas;
+- security schemes and per-operation permissions;
+- scope, confirmation, idempotency, safety, and deprecation extensions;
+- module and capability versions;
+- disabled modules omitted from paths and components when safe to do so.
+
+Contract tests compare registry operations, paths, OpenAPI operation IDs, SDK methods, and MCP tools.
+
+## Versioning
+
+`v1` is the transport major version. Function capability versions are returned independently. A breaking transport change uses a new base path. Additive capability changes remain in the same transport version. Deprecations declare replacement and sunset metadata but do not fabricate dates when no policy exists.

+# Self-hosting and operations
+
+## Deployment model
+
+Super Console is a SvelteKit server application deployed alongside network-reachable Superfunction services. An installation may run in one process for development or bind remote service clients, but module registration remains explicit and server-only.
+
+## Required configuration
+
+- public origin and trusted proxy settings;
+- AuthFn issuer/session/service-auth binding;
+- persistent administration state adapter;
+- audit and idempotency stores;
+- workspace/project/environment resolver;
+- explicit enabled module list and each module's service adapter;
+- SecFn-backed secret references where configured;
+- McpFn transport/auth configuration when MCP is enabled;
+- WatchFn/LogFn observability binding;
+- retention, rate limit, payload, pagination, and timeout limits.
+
+Secrets must be provided through the deployment secret mechanism or SecFn references. They are not placed in a client-visible module manifest.
+
+## Startup
+
+On startup the server:
+
+1. loads configuration;
+2. binds service adapters;
+3. validates manifests, dependencies, nested ownership, paths, tools, schemas, and safety metadata;
+4. verifies required persistence capabilities;
+5. initializes AuthFn, policy, audit, idempotency, observability, REST/OpenAPI, and McpFn adapters;
+6. exposes readiness only after the registry is valid.
+
+Invalid configuration fails closed with a sanitized error and detailed local server log.
+
+## Health
+
+- liveness reports process health without dependency detail;
+- readiness reports whether authentication, registry, required stores, and required module dependencies can serve traffic;
+- module health appears only to authorized operators;
+- optional module degradation does not make the whole installation unready unless configured as required;
+- health never exposes credentials, tenant data, or internal network addresses to anonymous callers.
+
+## Persistence and backup
+
+Back up:
+
+- AuthFn identity and membership state;
+- console policy/configuration state not stored as code;
+- durable audit events;
+- idempotency records for their retention window;
+- function-owned databases and object storage according to each function's runbook;
+- encryption keys through the deployment's secure key backup procedure.
+
+Test restores in an isolated environment. Audit ordering and tenant identifiers must survive restore. A backup without object storage or encryption keys is not a complete FileFn/MailFn/RecFn recovery.
+
+## Upgrade
+
+1. review transport and function capability versions;
+2. validate the new registry against configuration before traffic switch;
+3. run schema/provisioning plans supplied by owning functions;
+4. deploy with backward-compatible REST/OpenAPI where possible;
+5. verify authentication, tenant selection, audit, enabled module discovery, and representative reads;
+6. switch traffic;
+7. retain rollback artifacts and compatible data backups.
+
+Removing a module intentionally removes its UI/API/MCP exposure but does not delete domain data. Destructive decommissioning is a separate explicit operation.
+
+## Scaling
+
+Multi-process deployments require shared durable audit and idempotency stores. Sticky sessions must not substitute for durable correctness. Streaming logs, traces, or run updates use bounded connections and backpressure. Operation timeouts and pagination limits are configurable within safe server maxima.
+
+## Incident response
+
+- correlate reports by request and audit ID;
+- inspect WatchFn metrics/traces/errors, LogFn logs, and CatchFn feedback inside the WatchFn module;
+- revoke compromised AuthFn sessions/service credentials;
+- rotate secrets through SecFn/owning provider service;
+- disable a module in deployment configuration when containment requires it;
+- preserve audit and relevant artifacts before destructive remediation;
+- record correction actions as new audit events.
+
+## Development mode
+
+A local development configuration may use in-memory services and stores only when clearly marked and bound to loopback. It must still use the real registry, dispatcher, policy, schemas, REST/OpenAPI, SDK, MCP projection, and UIFn shell; it is not a separate mocked product architecture.

+# Architecture decisions
+
+## ADR-001 — One modular control plane
+
+**Decision:** Build one Super Console shell rather than independent dashboards.
+
+**Reason:** Authentication, tenancy, policy, audit, navigation, accessibility, deployment, and cross-function investigations are shared concerns. Function-owned manifests preserve modularity.
+
+## ADR-002 — Explicit registration
+
+**Decision:** Modules are enabled only through server-side deployment configuration.
+
+**Reason:** Credential presence and package installation are unsafe implicit activation signals. One explicit registry can mechanically remove disabled UI/API/MCP exposure.
+
+## ADR-003 — Function-owned admin services
+
+**Decision:** Each function owns its transport-neutral admin package and injected domain-service contract.
+
+**Reason:** The console must not become a second implementation of billing, auth, workflows, storage, search, or other domain logic.
+
+## ADR-004 — Shared kernel and projection
+
+**Decision:** REST/OpenAPI, TypeScript, MCP, and SvelteKit delegate to the same registry dispatcher.
+
+**Reason:** Separate handlers would drift in authorization, validation, errors, idempotency, and audit.
+
+## ADR-005 — SvelteKit, Tailwind, and UIFn
+
+**Decision:** Use SvelteKit and Tailwind configured through UIFn, with UIFn as the exclusive visual system.
+
+**Reason:** This matches the selected stack and strengthens the ecosystem's own Svelte UI layer. UIFn problems are product problems and are fixed at source.
+
+## ADR-006 — Operator/customer separation
+
+**Decision:** Do not merge customer-facing portals or widgets into Super Console.
+
+**Reason:** Their actors, information architecture, security boundaries, and tasks differ even when they share domain contracts and UIFn primitives.
+
+## ADR-007 — Universal tenancy
+
+**Decision:** Use workspace → project → environment, with optional function namespace and region execution attributes.
+
+**Reason:** A common hierarchy enables consistent navigation and policy while preserving DataFn/SearchFn/AuthFn regional and namespaced isolation.
+
+## ADR-008 — Nested ownership
+
+**Decision:** CatchFn and LogFn live under WatchFn; ContentFn lives under CmsFn.
+
+**Reason:** Their operator jobs and existing repository boundaries place investigation in observability and content data in the authoring studio, avoiding redundant top-level products.
+
+## ADR-009 — McpFn for administration MCP
+
+**Decision:** Project eligible registry operations through McpFn, including authorized mutations.
+
+**Reason:** McpFn supplies protocol contracts and testability; sharing dispatcher semantics prevents agent-specific authorization or audit gaps.
+
+## ADR-010 — Merge committed dev, observe dirty dev
+
+**Decision:** Merge fetched `origin/dev` into local `next`, then treat the uncommitted local `dev` diff as read-only forward-compatibility input.
+
+**Reason:** The committed branch contains newer BillFn/ApiFn/AuthFn/DataFn/FileFn/SearchFn work required by the user. Dirty work is user-owned, incomplete, and cannot be silently moved or committed.
+
+## ADR-011 — Self-hosted only
+
+**Decision:** No hosted control-plane dependency.
+
+**Reason:** The stated product boundary is a self-hosted stack. Deployment adapters and durable stores remain configurable.
+
+## ADR-012 — Initial SDK scope
+
+**Decision:** Ship TypeScript plus language-neutral REST/OpenAPI; defer Python administration SDK generation.
+
+**Reason:** It satisfies current consumption needs while keeping other languages unblocked by a stable wire contract.

content.text:
I think the audit is substantially correct. The right verdict is: **NO-GO for closing SFN-21, but GO as a strong platform-foundation milestone.**

The distinction matters. The branch contains a credible administration kernel, registry, SvelteKit/UIFn shell, REST/OpenAPI projection, MCP integration, and security hardening. But the [SFN-21 acceptance criteria](https://linear.app/21n/issue/SFN-21/build-super-console-as-the-modular-self-hosted-administration-control) explicitly require real function-owned integrations and representative operations—not only manifests that forward `operationId` and `input: unknown` to an injected executor.

My previous phrase “implemented end-to-end” was too strong. The handoff did disclose the generic-domain-schema boundary, but it should have characterized the result as “the complete shared platform and module inventory scaffold,” not the completed product.

The strongest audit findings are:

- **P1-01/P1-02/P1-05:** Correct and decisive. The 29 packages describe the administration surface but do not bind it to actual product services. CiFn is visually migrated, but the real control-plane workflows are not. Narrow operation IDs are useful, but an SDK with `unknown` inputs/results is not the promised typed SDK.
- **P1-04:** A genuine kernel correctness blocker. Returning failure after the domain mutation committed, while leaving an idempotency claim unresolved, creates exactly the ambiguity idempotency is supposed to prevent.
- **P1-03:** Correct against the attached architecture. The source requires every scope identifier, while the architecture explicitly defines installation-, workspace-, project-, and environment-scoped capabilities.
- **P2-01/P2-02/P2-04:** Solid findings and comparatively inexpensive to fix: contextual-policy-aware discovery, implicit outward secret defense, and startup regex validation.
- **P2-03:** The risk review is necessary, although “requires confirmation” should be decided per domain. Some operations may need MFA, approval, or typed intent binding rather than a generic confirmation dialog.

A few qualifications:

- “Zero real integrations” is slightly too broad. AuthFn sessions/CSRF/2FA, McpFn projection, and UIFn are real integrations. The accurate statement is **zero real product-admin domain bindings**.
- Fixture-backed Playwright probes are normal and useful. The problem is treating that probe as proof of the actual CiFn migration.
- Several findings share one root cause. P1-01, P1-02, P1-05, and P2-05 are separate acceptance failures, but not four independent architectural defects.
- P1-04’s remediation should not mandate a distributed transaction across arbitrary systems. A durable operation-state machine, execution receipt/outbox, leased claims, and reconciliation protocol could satisfy the requirement.

My recommended response is to accept the [audit](https://linear.app/21n/document/sfn-21-super-console-full-read-only-audit-2026-08-13-4fada346ba0b), keep SFN-21 **In Progress**, and proceed in this order:

1. Fix mutation outcome recovery, scope semantics, response redaction, policy-aware discovery, and schema validation.
2. Fully integrate reference verticals: AuthFn, CiFn, WatchFn/CatchFn/LogFn, CmsFn/ContentFn, then one billing, messaging, and security module.
3. Turn those implementations into the exact function-owned adapter pattern for the remaining modules.
4. Replace generic action envelopes with domain schemas and generate genuinely typed clients.
5. Add real service-bound tenancy and cross-surface tests, then refresh portable verification evidence.

I would not weaken SFN-21’s acceptance criteria to bless the current branch. The foundation is worth preserving, but the audit correctly identifies that the remaining work is product semantics, not polish.

I agree with the new audit. It is a credible **NO-GO**, and it correctly overturns my earlier PASS assessment.

I checked the live [SFN-21 issue](https://linear.app/21n/issue/SFN-21/build-super-console-as-the-modular-self-hosted-administration-control), its Architecture document, and the source at audited HEAD `f46cf63f`. The findings are well-supported.

Most importantly:

- **RA-P1-01 is decisive.** The live issue requires the complete required and optional module set. Our local documents unilaterally weakened that contract by allowing six unavailable modules. HostFn and UserFn are required but absent; ApiFn, BotFn, DocsFn, and LangFn are optional but unusable. Truthful incompleteness is preferable to fake adapters, but it is still incomplete.
- **RA-P1-02 is valid.** Several named SDK clients discard the shared capability client’s `operations`, `availability`, `invoke`, and `pages`. The shared client also lacks the required typed scope selector, deterministic timeout composition, and raw-response access.
- **RA-P2-01 is valid.** `finalizeAudit` is optional, startup does not require it, and replay recovery can therefore emit repeated terminal success events indefinitely.
- **RA-P2-02 is a real security issue.** One-time secret exceptions are key-name based globally, so allowing `token` permits every nested `token`, not one schema-bound path such as `item.token`.
- **RA-P2-03 is valid.** MailFn credential rotation creates a replacement and revokes the existing credential without confirmation or step-up authentication.
- **RA-P3-01 is valid.** The PASS completion report and “Blockers: None” contradict the unchanged Linear contract and the branch’s own six-module unavailable inventory. The browser probe was useful, but its artifacts are ephemeral rather than durable review evidence.

Two minor nuances do not change the verdict:

- The live issue enumerates 20 standalone required modules while saying “21 required”; that counting ambiguity should be cleaned up, but HostFn/UserFn are unquestionably required.
- Returning a narrower named SDK client is not inherently wrong, but it is wrong against SFN-21’s required uniform SDK contract and our own SDK documentation.

My recommended remediation order would be:

1. Correct the local completion/tracker status to **BLOCKED/NO-GO**.
2. Fix audit reconciliation, path-specific one-time secrets, and MailFn confirmation.
3. Complete the SDK contract uniformly across every available module.
4. Implement the six missing modules—or explicitly revise and re-approve the live Linear acceptance contract.
5. Preserve sanitized browser evidence durably and rerun all gates on the exact final HEAD.
6. Re-audit that commit.

The [re-audit](https://linear.app/21n/document/sfn-21-super-console-read-only-re-audit-2026-08-13-158d05a7f697) is materially better calibrated than our completion report. I would use its eight exit criteria as the next implementation checklist. I made no repository or Linear changes during this assessment.

name: pr-refetch-fix
description: Refetch the latest GitHub PR review feedback reliably before applying fixes. Use when a user asks to re-check review comments after a push, says there are newer PR comments that were missed, or when timestamp-only PR comment queries may be incomplete or misleading. This skill is for GitHub PR review triage where unresolved review threads, inline comments, review bodies, and issue comments must be checked together.
---

# PR Refetch Fix

Refetch PR feedback from the right GitHub surfaces before deciding there are no new issues. Do not rely only on a timestamp cutoff against inline review comments.

## Core Rule

When the user asks for "newer PR comments", "latest review issues", or says comments were missed:

1. Check current unresolved review threads first.
2. Treat timestamp filtering as secondary, not primary.
3. Verify every still-open thread against the current worktree before fixing or dismissing it.

The failure mode this skill prevents is:

- querying only `pulls/{n}/comments` after an incorrect cutoff time
- missing comments posted in review threads or review bodies
- missing still-unresolved older threads that remain actionable after newer pushes

## Workflow

### 1. Identify the PRs and auth context

Use the user's existing GitHub auth context if they specified one earlier, such as:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other
```

Preserve that context for every `gh` call in the workflow.

### 1a. Work only in the PR's corresponding worktree and branch

Before checking comments or making fixes:

1. switch to the PR's dedicated worktree
2. confirm the checked-out branch is the PR head branch
3. inspect and edit only in that worktree

Do not:

- inspect comments against the main repo checkout if the PR has a separate worktree
- validate a review comment against `next`, `dev`, or another sibling PR branch
- make fixes in one worktree and assume they apply to another PR branch

If multiple PRs are involved, handle each PR in its own worktree independently.

Minimum check:

```bash
git branch --show-current
git status --short
git remote -v
```

Use the worktree that already backs the PR whenever available. Treat that worktree as the source of truth for:

- whether a comment is already fixed
- whether a thread is stale
- what code should be edited

### 2. Do not start with timestamp-only filtering

Do not begin with:

- only `gh pr view --json comments`
- only `gh api repos/.../pulls/<n>/comments`
- only "comments after last pushed commit time"

Those can miss actionable review feedback.

### 3. Fetch unresolved review threads with GraphQL

This is the primary source of truth for "what still needs attention".

Use:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh api graphql -f query='
query {
  repository(owner:"OWNER", name:"REPO") {
    pullRequest(number:PR_NUMBER) {
      reviewThreads(first:100) {
        nodes {
          isResolved
          path
          comments(first:20) {
            nodes {
              body
              author { login }
              createdAt
              outdated
              url
              diffHunk
              originalLine
              line
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}'
```

If there may be more than 100 threads, page through the connection instead of assuming the first page is complete.

### 4. Also check the other review surfaces

After review threads, inspect:

1. PR reviews
2. PR issue comments
3. Inline review comments if needed for raw export or extra metadata

Useful commands:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr view PR_NUMBER --repo OWNER/REPO --json reviews,comments,updatedAt,url
```

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/PR_NUMBER/comments
```

Use these to supplement threads, not replace them.

### 5. Use timestamps carefully

If the user explicitly wants "since the last push", compute the cutoff from the exact pushed commit, not a guessed time.

Rules:

- use the exact commit SHA that was pushed
- use its absolute timestamp in UTC
- if the user seems confused about "today", "after that push", or "latest", mention exact dates/times

Even with an accurate cutoff, do not exclude unresolved review threads just because the thread started earlier. A still-unresolved thread can remain actionable after later pushes.

### 6. Classify findings before editing

For each thread or comment:

`Actionable`
- thread is unresolved, and
- the comment still matches the current file state, and
- the issue is not already fixed in the worktree

`Already fixed / stale`
- thread is outdated, or
- the code already addresses it, or
- the comment refers to an earlier diff shape that no longer exists

`Non-code noise`
- Graphite merge queue comments
- usage-limit notices
- bot bookkeeping without code findings

### 7. Verify against the current worktree

Before editing:

1. open the current file in the worktree
2. inspect the exact code around the commented path/line
3. decide whether the review comment is still valid now

Do not trust the review diff alone. Many bot comments are attached to old hunks and become stale after subsequent pushes.

### 8. Fix only the valid items

When fixing:

- prefer narrow fixes tied to the still-valid review findings
- add focused regression coverage when practical
- keep unrelated local or `.conduct/` artifacts out of commits unless the user explicitly asks for them

### 9. Report with explicit buckets

Summarize findings as:

- `Fixed`
- `Skipped (Already Fixed)`
- `Not Attempted`

If something remains pending because of extracted-worktree dependency issues, say so explicitly.

## Decision Heuristics

Use unresolved threads as the main queue when the user says:

- "check newer PR comments"
- "there are still comments"
- "you missed some issues"
- "refetch review feedback"

Use timestamp filtering only to answer narrower questions like:

- "what comments arrived after commit <sha>?"
- "what was posted after the last push?"

Even then, compare the result against current unresolved threads before concluding there is nothing new.

## Common Pitfalls

- Missing comments because `gh pr view --json comments` does not include review threads.
- Missing comments because `pulls/<n>/comments` was queried with the wrong cutoff time.
- Treating all old comments as irrelevant even when the thread is still unresolved.
- Treating all unresolved bot comments as actionable without checking the current code.
- Forgetting that some PR activity is non-code noise, especially merge-queue comments.

## Minimum Successful Pass

A correct refetch pass should:

1. fetch unresolved review threads with GraphQL
2. inspect review bodies and issue comments
3. cross-check against the current worktree
4. separate valid issues from stale ones
5. only then start fixing code

# PR Refetch Fix

Refetch PR feedback from the right GitHub surfaces before deciding there are no new issues. Do not rely only on a timestamp cutoff against inline review comments.

## Core Rule

When the user asks for "newer PR comments", "latest review issues", or says comments were missed:

1. Check current unresolved review threads first.
2. Treat timestamp filtering as secondary, not primary.
3. Verify every still-open thread against the current worktree before fixing or dismissing it.

The failure mode this skill prevents is:

- querying only `pulls/{n}/comments` after an incorrect cutoff time
- missing comments posted in review threads or review bodies
- missing still-unresolved older threads that remain actionable after newer pushes

## Workflow

### 1. Identify the PRs and auth context

Use the user's existing GitHub auth context if they specified one earlier, such as:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other
```

Preserve that context for every `gh` call in the workflow.

### 1a. Work only in the PR's corresponding worktree and branch

Before checking comments or making fixes:

1. switch to the PR's dedicated worktree
2. confirm the checked-out branch is the PR head branch
3. inspect and edit only in that worktree

Do not:

- inspect comments against the main repo checkout if the PR has a separate worktree
- validate a review comment against `next`, `dev`, or another sibling PR branch
- make fixes in one worktree and assume they apply to another PR branch

If multiple PRs are involved, handle each PR in its own worktree independently.

Minimum check:

```bash
git branch --show-current
git status --short
git remote -v
```

Use the worktree that already backs the PR whenever available. Treat that worktree as the source of truth for:

- whether a comment is already fixed
- whether a thread is stale
- what code should be edited

### 2. Do not start with timestamp-only filtering

Do not begin with:

- only `gh pr view --json comments`
- only `gh api repos/.../pulls/<n>/comments`
- only "comments after last pushed commit time"

Those can miss actionable review feedback.

### 3. Fetch unresolved review threads with GraphQL

This is the primary source of truth for "what still needs attention".

Use:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh api graphql -f query='
query {
  repository(owner:"OWNER", name:"REPO") {
    pullRequest(number:PR_NUMBER) {
      reviewThreads(first:100) {
        nodes {
          isResolved
          path
          comments(first:20) {
            nodes {
              body
              author { login }
              createdAt
              outdated
              url
              diffHunk
              originalLine
              line
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}'
```

If there may be more than 100 threads, page through the connection instead of assuming the first page is complete.

### 4. Also check the other review surfaces

After review threads, inspect:

1. PR reviews
2. PR issue comments
3. Inline review comments if needed for raw export or extra metadata

Useful commands:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr view PR_NUMBER --repo OWNER/REPO --json reviews,comments,updatedAt,url
```

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/PR_NUMBER/comments
```

Use these to supplement threads, not replace them.

### 5. Use timestamps carefully

If the user explicitly wants "since the last push", compute the cutoff from the exact pushed commit, not a guessed time.

Rules:

- use the exact commit SHA that was pushed
- use its absolute timestamp in UTC
- if the user seems confused about "today", "after that push", or "latest", mention exact dates/times

Even with an accurate cutoff, do not exclude unresolved review threads just because the thread started earlier. A still-unresolved thread can remain actionable after later pushes.

### 6. Classify findings before editing

For each thread or comment:

`Actionable`
- thread is unresolved, and
- the comment still matches the current file state, and
- the issue is not already fixed in the worktree

`Already fixed / stale`
- thread is outdated, or
- the code already addresses it, or
- the comment refers to an earlier diff shape that no longer exists

`Non-code noise`
- Graphite merge queue comments
- usage-limit notices
- bot bookkeeping without code findings

### 7. Verify against the current worktree

Before editing:

1. open the current file in the worktree
2. inspect the exact code around the commented path/line
3. decide whether the review comment is still valid now

Do not trust the review diff alone. Many bot comments are attached to old hunks and become stale after subsequent pushes.

### 8. Fix only the valid items

When fixing:

- prefer narrow fixes tied to the still-valid review findings
- add focused regression coverage when practical
- keep unrelated local or `.conduct/` artifacts out of commits unless the user explicitly asks for them

### 9. Report with explicit buckets

Summarize findings as:

- `Fixed`
- `Skipped (Already Fixed)`
- `Not Attempted`

If something remains pending because of extracted-worktree dependency issues, say so explicitly.

## Decision Heuristics

Use unresolved threads as the main queue when the user says:

- "check newer PR comments"
- "there are still comments"
- "you missed some issues"
- "refetch review feedback"

Use timestamp filtering only to answer narrower questions like:

- "what comments arrived after commit <sha>?"
- "what was posted after the last push?"

Even then, compare the result against current unresolved threads before concluding there is nothing new.

## Common Pitfalls

- Missing comments because `gh pr view --json comments` does not include review threads.
- Missing comments because `pulls/<n>/comments` was queried with the wrong cutoff time.
- Treating all old comments as irrelevant even when the thread is still unresolved.
- Treating all unresolved bot comments as actionable without checking the current code.
- Forgetting that some PR activity is non-code noise, especially merge-queue comments.

## Minimum Successful Pass

A correct refetch pass should:

1. fetch unresolved review threads with GraphQL
2. inspect review bodies and issue comments
3. cross-check against the current worktree
4. separate valid issues from stale ones
5. only then start fixing code

</skill>

name: pr-refetch-fix
description: Refetch the latest GitHub PR review feedback reliably before applying fixes. Use when a user asks to re-check review comments after a push, says there are newer PR comments that were missed, or when timestamp-only PR comment queries may be incomplete or misleading. This skill is for GitHub PR review triage where unresolved review threads, inline comments, review bodies, and issue comments must be checked together.
---

# PR Refetch Fix

Refetch PR feedback from the right GitHub surfaces before deciding there are no new issues. Do not rely only on a timestamp cutoff against inline review comments.

## Core Rule

When the user asks for "newer PR comments", "latest review issues", or says comments were missed:

1. Check current unresolved review threads first.
2. Treat timestamp filtering as secondary, not primary.
3. Verify every still-open thread against the current worktree before fixing or dismissing it.

The failure mode this skill prevents is:

- querying only `pulls/{n}/comments` after an incorrect cutoff time
- missing comments posted in review threads or review bodies
- missing still-unresolved older threads that remain actionable after newer pushes

## Workflow

### 1. Identify the PRs and auth context

Use the user's existing GitHub auth context if they specified one earlier, such as:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other
```

Preserve that context for every `gh` call in the workflow.

### 1a. Work only in the PR's corresponding worktree and branch

Before checking comments or making fixes:

1. switch to the PR's dedicated worktree
2. confirm the checked-out branch is the PR head branch
3. inspect and edit only in that worktree

Do not:

- inspect comments against the main repo checkout if the PR has a separate worktree
- validate a review comment against `next`, `dev`, or another sibling PR branch
- make fixes in one worktree and assume they apply to another PR branch

If multiple PRs are involved, handle each PR in its own worktree independently.

Minimum check:

```bash
git branch --show-current
git status --short
git remote -v
```

Use the worktree that already backs the PR whenever available. Treat that worktree as the source of truth for:

- whether a comment is already fixed
- whether a thread is stale
- what code should be edited

### 2. Do not start with timestamp-only filtering

Do not begin with:

- only `gh pr view --json comments`
- only `gh api repos/.../pulls/<n>/comments`
- only "comments after last pushed commit time"

Those can miss actionable review feedback.

### 3. Fetch unresolved review threads with GraphQL

This is the primary source of truth for "what still needs attention".

Use:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh api graphql -f query='
query {
  repository(owner:"OWNER", name:"REPO") {
    pullRequest(number:PR_NUMBER) {
      reviewThreads(first:100) {
        nodes {
          isResolved
          path
          comments(first:20) {
            nodes {
              body
              author { login }
              createdAt
              outdated
              url
              diffHunk
              originalLine
              line
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}'
```

If there may be more than 100 threads, page through the connection instead of assuming the first page is complete.

### 4. Also check the other review surfaces

After review threads, inspect:

1. PR reviews
2. PR issue comments
3. Inline review comments if needed for raw export or extra metadata

Useful commands:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr view PR_NUMBER --repo OWNER/REPO --json reviews,comments,updatedAt,url
```

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/PR_NUMBER/comments
```

Use these to supplement threads, not replace them.

### 5. Use timestamps carefully

If the user explicitly wants "since the last push", compute the cutoff from the exact pushed commit, not a guessed time.

Rules:

- use the exact commit SHA that was pushed
- use its absolute timestamp in UTC
- if the user seems confused about "today", "after that push", or "latest", mention exact dates/times

Even with an accurate cutoff, do not exclude unresolved review threads just because the thread started earlier. A still-unresolved thread can remain actionable after later pushes.

### 6. Classify findings before editing

For each thread or comment:

`Actionable`
- thread is unresolved, and
- the comment still matches the current file state, and
- the issue is not already fixed in the worktree

`Already fixed / stale`
- thread is outdated, or
- the code already addresses it, or
- the comment refers to an earlier diff shape that no longer exists

`Non-code noise`
- Graphite merge queue comments
- usage-limit notices
- bot bookkeeping without code findings

### 7. Verify against the current worktree

Before editing:

1. open the current file in the worktree
2. inspect the exact code around the commented path/line
3. decide whether the review comment is still valid now

Do not trust the review diff alone. Many bot comments are attached to old hunks and become stale after subsequent pushes.

### 8. Fix only the valid items

When fixing:

- prefer narrow fixes tied to the still-valid review findings
- add focused regression coverage when practical
- keep unrelated local or `.conduct/` artifacts out of commits unless the user explicitly asks for them

### 9. Report with explicit buckets

Summarize findings as:

- `Fixed`
- `Skipped (Already Fixed)`
- `Not Attempted`

If something remains pending because of extracted-worktree dependency issues, say so explicitly.

## Decision Heuristics

Use unresolved threads as the main queue when the user says:

- "check newer PR comments"
- "there are still comments"
- "you missed some issues"
- "refetch review feedback"

Use timestamp filtering only to answer narrower questions like:

- "what comments arrived after commit <sha>?"
- "what was posted after the last push?"

Even then, compare the result against current unresolved threads before concluding there is nothing new.

## Common Pitfalls

- Missing comments because `gh pr view --json comments` does not include review threads.
- Missing comments because `pulls/<n>/comments` was queried with the wrong cutoff time.
- Treating all old comments as irrelevant even when the thread is still unresolved.
- Treating all unresolved bot comments as actionable without checking the current code.
- Forgetting that some PR activity is non-code noise, especially merge-queue comments.

## Minimum Successful Pass

A correct refetch pass should:

1. fetch unresolved review threads with GraphQL
2. inspect review bodies and issue comments
3. cross-check against the current worktree
4. separate valid issues from stale ones
5. only then start fixing code
